top_articles.title: DevFest is back!

top_articles.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation

Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

top_articles.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec

top_articles.title: Step by Step guide: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK

Developers can use streaming tools to yield progress updates or background execution patterns to keep conversations fluid during long-running backend queries. Additionally, configuring response scheduling behaviors such as WHEN_IDLE, INTERRUPT, or SILENT gives developers precise control over when and how tool results are delivered into the conversation.

top_articles.title: Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens
top_articles.summary: Google OAuth Platform now supports DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) to sender-constrain refresh tokens, neutralizing Infostealer malware and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. By cryptographically binding long-lived refresh tokens while maintaining short-lived access tokens as standard Bearer tokens, developers achieve robust credential security without incurring high-QPS API performance overhead. Additionally, developers integrating multi-agent or Model Context Protocol (MCP) workloads can use Google Cloud Secure Token Service (STS) to handle secure token delegation across agent chains.

Security.title: RAG chunking, measured: heading-aware chunks doubled hit@1 on the FastAPI docs
Security.summary:
Chunking is the first decision in a RAG pipeline and the one people tune least. Most projects take the default of their framework, often fixed-size chunks with overlap, and move on. I wanted numbers, so I ran five strategies over a real documentation set and measured how often retrieval finds the right section.

Result: splitting at headings first, then packing paragraphs, raised hit@1 from 0.39 to 0.71. Adding the heading path to each chunk raised it again to 0.79.

The test

  • Corpus: the English FastAPI docs, 151 Markdown files with 1.45 million characters. Real technical writing, with headings, code blocks and admonitions.
  • Queries: every h2/h3 heading with at least 300 characters of body and 2+ words. That gave 773 queries, such as "Declare request example data" or "Dependencies with yield and except".
  • Correct answer: a retrieved chunk counts as a hit when at least half of its text lies inside the section that heading introduces.
  • Retriever: BM25 (k1=1.5, b=0.75). It is deterministic and needs no API key, so anyone can reproduce the numbers exactly.

Strategies

  1. Fixed 800/100: 800-character windows with 100 characters of overlap. The classic default.
  2. Fixed 530/100: the same, but sized to match the heading-aware chunks, as a control.
  3. Paragraph-packed 800: greedily pack blank-line-separated paragraphs up to 800 characters. This is roughly what "recursive" splitters do.
  4. Heading-aware: split at every heading first, so a chunk never contains two sections, then paragraph-pack within the section.
  5. Heading-aware + heading path: the same chunks, with Page title > Section > Subsection prepended to the text that gets indexed.

Results

Strategy Chunks Avg chars Crosses a section Splits a code block hit@1 hit@5 MRR
Fixed 800/100 2,142 770 58.8% 7.3% 0.389 0.611 0.477
Fixed 530/100 (size-matched) 3,446 516 47.5% 6.1% 0.481 0.766 0.598
Paragraph-packed 800 1,737 835 57.2% 3.6% 0.375 0.576 0.455
Heading-aware 2,713 534 0.0% 2.1% 0.712 0.933 0.804
Heading-aware + heading path 2,713 534 0.0% 2.1% 0.785 0.966 0.859

What the numbers say

More than half of fixed-size chunks straddle two sections. A chunk that is half "Install" and half "Configuration" is a mediocre match for both. That shows up directly as lower retrieval scores.

Smaller chunks help, but not as much as structure. The size-matched control improved on the 800-character default (hit@5 0.61 → 0.77), which confirms part of the gain is simply size. But heading-aware chunks of the same average size scored 0.93. The remaining gap comes from respecting section boundaries.

Paragraph packing alone didn't help. It halves the number of broken code blocks, which is nice for answer quality, but its chunks cross sections just as often as fixed windows do.

The heading path is cheap recall. A chunk from the middle of a long section often doesn't repeat the words of its title. Prepending Tutorial > Security > OAuth2 scopes gives every chunk that context. It cost nothing and added 7 points of hit@1.

Honest caveats

  • Heading-as-query favors heading-aware chunking. Real user questions are phrased differently from section titles. The direction of the result should hold, but expect smaller gaps with real queries.
  • The hit rule rewards staying inside one section. That is the point I'm testing, but a chunk that crosses sections and still contains the answer counts as a miss here.
  • BM25, not embeddings. Dense retrievers are more forgiving of wording. Section-crossing chunks still dilute an embedding across two topics, so I expect the same ranking, but run it on your own stack.
  • Markdown makes this easy. For PDFs you first need to recover headings (font size, bold, numbering). That extraction step is worth the effort.

A heading-aware chunker in 30 lines 

import re

HEADING = re.compile(r"^(#{1,3}) (.+?)\s*(\{.*\})?$", re.M)
SIZE = 800

def sections(text):
    """Yield (start, end, 'Page > Section > Sub') for each heading."""
    ms = list(HEADING.finditer(text))
    stack = []
    if not ms or ms[0].start() > 0:
        yield 0, ms[0].start() if ms else len(text), ""
    for i, m in enumerate(ms):
        level, title = len(m.group(1)), m.group(2).strip()
        stack = [s for s in stack if s[0] < level] + [(level, title)]
        end = ms[i + 1].start() if i + 1 < len(ms) else len(text)
        yield m.start(), end, " > ".join(t for _, t in stack)

def pack(text):
    """Greedily pack blank-line paragraphs up to SIZE characters."""
    out, start, cur = [], 0, 0
    for m in re.finditer(r"\n\s*\n", text):
        if m.end() - start > SIZE and cur > start:
            out.append(text[start:cur]); start = cur
        cur = m.end()
    out.append(text[start:])
    return [c for c in out if c.strip()]

def chunk(text):
    for s, e, path in sections(text):
        for body in pack(text[s:e]):
            yield {"text": body, "embed_text": f"{path}\n{body}" if path else body, "section": path}

Store text for display and citations. Embed and index embed_text.

What I'd do in your pipeline

  1. Never let a chunk cross a heading. It is the single biggest win in this test.
  2. Prepend the heading path to what you embed and index, not to what you show the user.
  3. Keep chunks around 500 characters for technical docs, then tune with your own eval set.
  4. Measure it. Generate queries from your own headings like I did here, and you have a free retrieval regression test in under an hour.

The full benchmark script (BM25 from scratch, all five strategies, metrics, about 90 lines of standard-library Python) is on the original post. The follow-up, which fuses these chunks' BM25 ranks with vectors, is hybrid search with RRF, alpha swept 0 to 1.

Project: https://github.com/vedhanth66/Lokantra

Tagline: PREDICT the UNPREDICTABLE.

Developed LOKĀNTRA, an AI-powered simulation platform that transforms real-world documents and scenarios into interactive knowledge graphs and simulated social environments populated by AI agents.

The platform explores how different stakeholders might react to events, influence one another, and collectively shape possible outcomes. Rather than relying on a single LLM-generated prediction, it combines multi-agent simulation, graph-based knowledge retrieval, intelligent decision routing, and evidence-grounded reporting.

KEY ENGINEERING CONTRIBUTIONS AND FEATURES

  1. Knowledge Graph Engineering: Implemented dynamic ontology generation and document-to-knowledge-graph pipelines using TigerGraph and Zep Cloud.

  2. Multi-Agent AI Simulation: Integrated CAMEL-AI and OASIS to create simulated personas and model interactions across Reddit-style and Twitter-style environments.

  3. Cognitive Swarm Routing: Developed a hierarchical decision architecture combining heuristic reflex gating, LAYA System 1 decision intelligence, and LLM-based reasoning.

  4. Neuromorphic Computing Research: Explored BrainChip Akida-inspired spiking neural network reflex gating as an experimental approach to reducing unnecessary agent computations.

  5. Graph-Based Memory and Retrieval: Integrated graph-backed memory and retrieval mechanisms to provide contextual information for simulation analysis.

  6. Agent Interrogation: Enabled users to interview individual simulated agents and investigate the reasoning behind their decisions, opinions, and reactions.

  7. Autonomous Report Generation: Developed a tool-assisted ReportAgent that retrieves simulation evidence, generates structured analytical reports, supports follow-up conversations, and exports PDFs.

  8. Token-Aware Processing: Implemented representative document chunking, context management, staged generation, and decision-tier telemetry to help optimize LLM usage.

  9. Voice-Based Input: Integrated a configurable Sarvam AI Saaras speech-to-text pipeline for natural-language scenario input.

  10. Enterprise Integration Research: Incorporated viaSocket MCP configuration for external integrations and human-in-the-loop action workflows.

TECHNOLOGY STACK

Python, Flask, Vue.js 3, Vite, JavaScript, TigerGraph, Zep Cloud, GraphRAG, CAMEL-AI, OASIS, LAYA, BrainChip Akida (experimental), OpenAI-compatible LLM APIs, Sarvam AI, Supabase, D3.js, MCP, viaSocket, Docker.

CORE VISION

Move beyond static AI predictions towards interactive simulations where users can explore possible futures, investigate individual perspectives, and understand the dynamics behind emerging outcomes.

Frontend.title: Graveyard: a funeral for dead code, with a checker that keeps the AI honest
Frontend.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Graveyard is a funeral for dead code. Every repo has a graveyard: files deleted with a commit message like "fix stuff" and never thought about again. For the Ghost in the Machine theme, I wanted to dig them up and give each one a tombstone.

A small Node script reads a git repo's history (read-only) and exports every deleted file as JSON. The page then draws a candlelit cemetery with one tombstone per file: born, died, an epitaph, and the real commit message that killed it. The idea is that a local open-weight model, Gemma 3 4B through Ollama, writes the epitaph and the cause of death.

My reading of the theme: the ghost in the machine is the AI inventing a backstory for something that can't correct it. So the part I spent the most time on is a checker that stops the model from making things up.

  • Dates, file names and commit hashes come from the repo, never from the model.
  • The "cause of death" has to share most of its key words with the real commit message, or it is replaced with "Cause of death unknown" and marked "Unverified claim removed".
  • An epitaph that mentions a number, date or hash that isn't in the data is replaced with a plain one.

Demo

Live demo (fake data, canned text, no model): https://p44-code.github.io/graveyard/

In the demo, one tombstone has a cause of death I planted on purpose. Its real commit message is just "fix stuff", but the canned answer talks about memory leaks. The checker catches it, shows "Cause of death unknown", and prints the original commit message underneath.

An important note: the online demo uses canned text, not model output. GitHub Pages can't run Ollama on your computer, so the live demo only shows the page and the checker.

Code

P44-code / graveyard

⚰️ Graveyard: A Funeral for Dead Code

"Theme: Ghost in the Machine — Memorializing the code we wrote, loved, refactored, and purged."

Graveyard is a solemn, client-side digital cemetery for retired source code files. It transforms Git deletion logs into atmospheric, Gothic terminal tombstones commemorating deprecated shims, abandoned hacks, and forgotten features.

Built for open-source AI challenges with a strict security-first architecture:

  • Zero Frameworks, Zero Build Step, Zero NPM Runtime Dependencies: Pure HTML5, CSS3, and ES modules.
  • Strict Content-Security-Policy: Enforced via meta tags (connect-src locked exclusively to 'self' and http://localhost:11434).
  • Open-Weight Models Only: Runs locally through Ollama with Google's open-weight Gemma (gemma3:4b). No cloud models, no API keys, and no telemetry.
  • Honest Verifier: Automatically detects model hallucinations, requiring at least 60% keyword match against Git commit logs before verifying cause-of-death claims.

🏛️ Modes of Operation

  1. Demo Mode (Default & Offline)
    • Built-in…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. The README explains how to run Demo mode and Local mode.

How I Built It

  • Model: Gemma 3 4B (gemma3:4b), an open-weight model, served locally through Ollama. The app calls only http://localhost:11434. A guard in the code throws if the model name doesn't start with "gemma", and there are no API keys anywhere in the app.
  • App: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No framework, no build step, no npm dependencies. A strict Content-Security-Policy, and all text is rendered with textContent, never innerHTML.
  • Export script: a Node script with no dependencies that runs read-only git commands and writes graveyard.json.
  • Safety: commit messages and code are treated as untrusted text. They are wrapped in delimiters in the prompt, and the model's output can only fill text fields. It can't change dates, hashes or settings. This reduces prompt-injection risk but doesn't remove it, since a 4B model can still be fooled.
  • Tests: 15 unit tests for the checker, all passing.

I used Google AI Studio's builder (a closed Gemini model) for the first version of the code, and an AI assistant to plan and review it. Then I audited what I got. The builder had added a Gemini API key template, a Gemini config file and a Gemini library to a project that was meant to be Gemma only. The app never used them, but I deleted them. In review we also found a bug in my checker: it read the word "dead" as a commit hash, because d, e, a and d are valid hex letters. In an app about dead code, that matters. It is fixed.

What did not work

On my laptop, Local mode reached Ollama, but the first response timed out after 60 seconds. My machine is slow, and I ran out of time to raise the timeout and retest. So I never saw Gemma write a real eulogy for a real file in this project, and the model-writing path is untested end to end. I'm saying this plainly because the checker's whole point is not to claim things that weren't verified. For the same reason I'm not claiming it works offline.

Other limits

  • The checker compares words, not meaning. "Removed" versus "added" could still pass.
  • A vague commit message copied word for word still passes as "paraphrased". That is the next thing I would fix.
  • Tested on Windows only.

To try Local mode: install Ollama, run ollama pull gemma3:4b, set OLLAMA_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173, and on a slow machine raise OLLAMA_TIMEOUT_MS in modules/adapters.js.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Deleted code is often private code. Pasting it into a closed cloud API means trusting someone else's server with your repo's history. With an open-weight model running locally, the design keeps everything on your own machine: no API key, no account, no bill, and the app only talks to localhost.

I want to be careful here. I only tested on a fake repo, and I never completed a Local run, so this is a benefit of the design, not something I proved on a real private codebase. What I can say honestly is that open models are what make that design possible at all. A hosted API would have broken the "your code stays with you" idea from the start.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: the app is built around Gemma 3 4B served locally through Ollama, with a guard that refuses any non-Gemma model. As described above, I did not complete a full Local run, so I understand if this one is a long shot.

Frontend.title: Addendum R2: La tasa que faltaba, medida sobre las dos clases que faltaban
Frontend.summary:
Addendum R2 — la tasa que faltaba, medida sobre las dos clases que faltaban

Este artículo sustituye como lectura al anterior —«Addendum: corregí mi propio instrumento y el número bajó de
807 a 612»: https://dev.to/alexisromtz7/addendum-corregi-mi-propio-instrumento-y-el-numero-bajo-de-807-a-612-5172—
cuyo cuerpo se publicó sin el Markdown con que fue escrito: la plataforma guardó el texto y descartó la sintaxis.
El contenido es el mismo; la forma no. Se republica para que se pueda leer lo que se midió. El original sigue vivo y
sin editar, como registro de lo que el entorno de publicación hizo con él (§9).

Este documento no reescribe el anterior. El addendum publicado con RC 2 y RC 4
(ADDENDUM_ARTICULO_20261030.md, blob 723dda49, vivo en Dev.to) queda intacto byte a byte, porque un acto
público no se corrige por edición: se corrige por adenda. Lo que sigue sustituye solo su sección «La tasa que
faltaba», y solo en la parte que dejó abierta.

Huella de esta revisión: HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-TPR-RC1-RC5-20261030. Se declara como texto en código y no como
comentario HTML por la razón medida en §9.

1. Lo que quedaba abierto, dicho con la cifra al lado

El addendum anterior cerró la tasa de RC 2 y RC 4: 33 casos, 100% formal, 15.2% sustantiva. Y declaró su
propio residuo en la misma página: RC 1 (60) y RC 5 (308) seguían sin tasa.

Eso significa que 368 de las 612 observaciones publicadas — el 60,1% del numerador — no tenían veredicto. Un
cliente que preguntara «¿cuál es tu tasa de falsos positivos?» recibía una respuesta que valía para 33 casos y se
presentaba como si valiera para 612. Esa era la debilidad, y no estaba escondida: estaba escrita.

Ya no está abierta.

2. La medición

Misma disciplina que la vez anterior, y en el mismo orden: primero la predicción, después la lectura.

Se escribió un pre-registro (preregistro_tpr_rc1_rc5_20261030.json, 129 líneas, blob 05eaead8) con las clases
sustantivas, el sesgo declarado y cinco falsadores, antes de abrir un solo run: o un solo uses:. Después se
re-descargaron los 163 archivos de workflow del lote por blob SHA desde la API de GitHub y se verificó su
sha256 contra el manifiesto: 163/163 idénticos, 0 fallos. El motor reprodujo el reparto exacto:
RC 1 60 · RC 2 30 · RC 4 3 · RC 5 308.

clase lectura resultado
RC 5 REF_MUTABLE ¿el uses: citado existe en el crudo y su ref es realmente flotante? 308/308, 0 falsos positivos
RC 1 AUTORIDAD_CONTAMINADA ¿el job tiene escritura y ejecuta código en la misma línea citada? 60/60, 0 falsos positivos
Control negativo RC 5 de 1321 uses:, 1013 están fijados a SHA de 40: ¿cuántos marca el motor? 0 de 1013
Control negativo RC 1 164 jobs ejecutan código de terceros sin scope de escritura: ¿cuántos marca? 0 de 164

Los dos controles negativos son la parte que importa. Un motor que marcara todo habría dado 1321 en lugar de 308, y
174 en lugar de 60. No los da: discrimina en los dos sentidos de la conjunción.

3. La tasa sustantiva: aquí es donde el número se encoge

Formal 100% no es la cifra que se puede vender, y el addendum anterior ya lo dijo para RC 2. Para RC 1 y RC 5
el efecto es mayor, porque estas dos clases se miden por ocurrencia y no por riesgo.

RC 5 — 308 ocurrencias no son 308 riesgos: son 31

El barrido de RC 5 no deduplica. Una misma acción repetida en veinte jobs produce veinte hallazgos. En los 163
archivos hay 1321 valores uses:, de los cuales 308 son flotantes… y esos 308 son solo 31 referencias
distintas. Publicar 308 sin decirlo sería inflar el numerador por la puerta de atrás.

clase ocurrencias distintas qué es
Primera parte (actions/*) 239 17 etiqueta móvil de GitHub sobre código de GitHub. Patrón documentado
Tercero, etiqueta flotante 42 5 pnpm/action-setup@v6, dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable, oven-sh/setup-bun@v2, rust-lang/crates-io-auth-action@v1, vercel/next.js/.github/actions/pr-auto-label@canary
Workflow reutilizable flotante 10 6 un workflow entero de otro repo ejecutado con el token de este
Placeholder sin sustituir 17 3 ver §4 — clase que la predicción no tenía
Imagen docker sin digest 0 0 predije 8; no hay una sola en los 10 repos

La superficie de terceros real: 52 ocurrencias y 11 referencias distintas — el 16,9% de las ocurrencias y el
35,5% de las distintas. Las otras 256 se reparten en 239 actions/*, que para un cliente es ruido (el control del
ref lo tiene GitHub, no el atacante que el cliente teme), y 17 placeholders que no resuelven y que van contados como
clase propia en §4, no como terceros.

Corrección con cadena (HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-CORRECCION-PORCENTAJE-TERCEROS-20261030). La primera versión de este
párrafo, escrita horas antes y nunca publicada, decía 22,4% y «las otras 239». Ese porcentaje es correcto para 69
ocurrencias, no para 52: la frase había sumado al numerador las 17 de R7, que son rutas $/.github/… del propio
repositorio del cliente y por tanto no son código de un tercero. La tabla de arriba nunca dijo 69; decía 42 + 10.
El número de la prosa y el de su propia tabla no medían lo mismo, y nada los comparaba. Se conserva el literal
equivocado a la vista porque un addendum que corrige cifras no puede editarse en silencio —esa es la misma regla que
lo hizo nacer—. La corrección viaja con el censo:
INVESTIGACION/evidencia/censo_tpr_rc1_rc5_20261030.json, campo superficie_de_terceros.correccion_con_cadena.

RC 1 — 60 hallazgos, 10 sostienen el nombre del código

RC 1 se llama AUTORIDAD_CONTAMINADA. La conjunción que mide —escritura y ejecución en el mismo job— es
correcta y da 60/60 formal. Pero solo una parte de esas 60 líneas ejerce o entrega la autoridad:

clase n qué es
A1 — escritura remota ejercida 9 gh run cancel, gh pr comment, gh api --method POST: el token es el instrumento de esa misma línea
A2 — descarga a ejecución 1 `curl https://rustwasm.github.io/…/init.sh -sSf \
A3 — hereda terceros 28 {% raw %}pnpm install, cargo build, npx -y firebase-tools@15.15.0, cargo binstall, gh corriendo con el token disponible
A4 — mutación local 5 git config sin push: la autoridad está declarada y no se ejerce
A5 — código del propio repo 11 pnpm run build, node scripts/…: el que ve el token es el dueño del repo
A7 — lexema sin ejecución 6 ver §4

Autoridad ejercida o entregada: 10 de 60 (16,7%). Ese es el número que la palabra «contaminada» puede defender.

4. Las dos clases que la predicción no tenía

En dos días consecutivos, el mismo patrón: la taxonomía se queda corta y la clase nueva aparece en el mismo lugar
donde el motor lee bien. Ayer fue NO_SUMIDERO (16 de 33). Hoy son dos, y las dos se declaran en vez de encajarse.

R7 — placeholder sin sustituir: 17 ocurrencias, 3 literales, 3 repositorios y 6 archivos. Los bytes crudos
contienen referencias locales escritas con el placeholder de plantilla de GitHub ($/…) que nunca se sustituyó:
$/.github/actions/setup 5 veces, todas en sveltejs/svelte ci.yml; $/.github/actions/issues-helper
11 veces en vitejs/vite —6 en bot.yml, 3 en issue-labeled.yml, 1 en issue-close-require.yml, 1 en
lock-closed-issues.yml—; y $/.github/workflows/notify-resolved-issues.yml 1 vez en nuxt/nuxt release.yml.
Los bytes son genuinos del origen: el git hash-object de los seis archivos coincide uno por uno con el blob_sha
que declara el manifiesto, así que no es un artefacto de la descarga. Su severidad queda NO_MEDIDO, por la misma
razón que NO_SUMIDERO: 0 si se lee que un uses que no resuelve no custodia nada, y «el hallazgo más fuerte» si se
lee que el archivo declara una intención que no ejecuta y quien lo audite creerá que está fijado. Resolverlo exige
saber si el repo genera ese archivo o lo commitea tal cual, y el archivo no lo dice.

Corrección con cadena (HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-R7-POR-ARCHIVO-20261030). La versión anterior de este párrafo, escrita
horas antes y nunca publicada, nombraba facebook/react como uno de los repositorios con placeholders. Medido sobre
los 163 workflows ya verificados por sha256: facebook/react tiene 26 workflows y cero ocurrencias, y los 17
están en svelte (5), vite (11) y nuxt (1). El conteo nunca cambió —17 ocurrencias, 3 literales—; la atribución
sí. Es el tercer caso del mismo defecto en la jornada: un campo estructurado correcto al lado de una frase que no
se deriva de él, igual que el 22,4% de §5. La corrección viaja con el censo, campo
clase_no_prevista.correccion_con_cadena.

A7 — el lexema casa sin que nada se ejecute: 6 de 60. Un echo " - NPM name: …" casa con el patrón de npm.
Un yq '.allowBuilds[]=false' -i pnpm-workspace.yaml casa porque el nombre del archivo dice pnpm. No es un
defecto del motor —su dominio declarado es léxico por línea— pero sí es ruido para un cliente, y por eso se cuenta
aparte y se publica: es la forma en que un falso positivo sobrevive a la corrección del motor.

5. Cuatro defectos del lector, encontrados antes de publicar

La lección de la vez anterior se aplicó con saña: el lector también se equivoca, y cuando se equivoca declara
culpable al instrumento correcto. Un lector independiente de mesa, sin el parser del motor, encontró cuatro:

  1. permissions: {} leído como {'{}': 'write'} → RC 1 inflado de 60 a 121 (61 falsos rojos).
  2. El uses: de job contado dos veces → RC 5 inflado de 308 a 319 (11 falsos rojos).
  3. Valores de permiso entrecomillados (contents: 'read') conservando las comillas → un job real quedaba fuera: 59 de 60.
  4. run: plegado en varias líneas leído solo en la primera → una línea citada aparecía truncada.

Los cuatro eran del lector. El motor no cambió una línea: su salida formal se sostiene 368/368.

6. Predicción contra medición, sin maquillar

predicción (pre-registrada) medido veredicto
RC 5: 308 TP, 0 FP, ±4 308 / 0 cumplida
RC 1: 60 TP, 0 FP, ±6 60 / 0 cumplida
31 a 60 literales distintos, punto 45 31 cumplida al borde, por un literal
Reparto RC 5: 240 / 55 / 8 / 3 / 2 / 0 239 / 42 / 0 / 10 / 0 / 17 dirección correcta, tres desvíos
Terceros distintos: 12 ± 6 11 cumplida
A1+A2: 9 ± 6 10 cumplida

Tres desvíos que se publican porque se midieron: la imagen docker sin digest no existe en los 10 repos (predije
8), el workflow reutilizable flotante es el triple de lo predicho (3 → 10, y es la clase más fuerte de las
cuatro), y apareció una clase que no estaba en la taxonomía (R7, 17). El punto de 45 contra 31 no es un fallo de
método: es la diferencia entre estimar cuántas ocurrencias habría y contar cuántas referencias distintas hay.

7. Lo que sigue sin tasa, y por qué se dice

SC1 — 211 observaciones, y no todas son la misma cosa. No son del gate: son el recuento de sustitución y cadena
del propio arnés. Con este acto se miden 368 de 612 observaciones (60,1%) — pero ese denominador no es el de
hallazgos, y confundirlos es el defecto que este addendum ya cometió una vez con otra cifra. De las 244 sin censo,
156 son REVIEW por diseño del contrato (SC1_JOB_WRITE_SCOPE_REVIEW 153 + SC1_ROOT_READ_ALL_REVIEW 3): son
inventario, no hallazgo, y no hay tasa que asignarles porque no afirman una vulnerabilidad. 55 sí son conjunción
real (SC1_ROOT_PERMISSIONS_MISSING 36 + SC1_ROOT_WRITE_INHERITED 19). Y 33 son la clase corregida (RC 2 30

  • RC 4 3), validada por revisión de dominio con cadena, no por censo. Sobre el denominador que un CTO querría —el de las que afirman una vulnerabilidad, 456— la cobertura es 368/456 = 80,7%, y lo que falta censar son 55 casos, el 9,0% del total, no 211. Lo que se publica como 60,1% sigue siendo correcto mientras el denominador sea «observaciones»; deja de serlo en cuanto el denominador es «hallazgos».

Huella de esta revisión: HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-DENOMINADOR-20261030 (§MEDICIÓN CON UNIDAD, aplicado al propio
enunciado: el 60,1% no estaba mal, estaba midiendo otra población).

Y tres residuos más, declarados: RC 5 emite job: '-', así que no dice qué job consume la acción y la
severidad por job queda NO_MEDIDA; el residuo propio del motor sigue vigente (env: con secretos + ejecución de
terceros sólo cae bajo RC 1 si hay scopes de escritura); y la lectura sustantiva es de mesa, sobre el YAML, sin
ejecutar los workflows: no mide si una acción de terceros es hostil hoy, mide si el ref es fijable y si la autoridad
se ejerce.

8. La frase que sí se puede publicar

612 observaciones, de las cuales 456 afirman una vulnerabilidad. Censadas: 368 — el 80,7% de los hallazgos y el
60,1% de las observaciones. De las 244 restantes: 156 son inventario REVIEW por contrato, 55 son conjunción
real sin censar y 33 son la clase corregida, validada por revisión de dominio.
TPR formal 368/368. Control negativo: 1013 refs fijadas sin marcar y 164 jobs sin escritura sin marcar.
Sustantiva: 10 de 60 hallazgos de autoridad ejercen o entregan la credencial; 11 referencias distintas de
terceros en 308 ocurrencias de ref flotante; 17 referencias que no resuelven —5 en sveltejs/svelte ci.yml,
11 en cuatro workflows de vitejs/vite (6 de ellas en bot.yml), 1 en nuxt/nuxt release.yml—, con
severidad NO_MEDIDO.

No hay un número redondo y no lo va a haber. Lo que hay es un instrumento que se equivocó 195 veces, lo publicó, se
corrigió, midió su propia tasa, encontró cuatro defectos en su lector y los publicó también, y dejó a la vista lo
que no pudo medir. Eso es lo que un CTO puede auditar. Un «1000 vulnerabilidades» no.

0 **, 0 comillas invertidas, 0 | y 0 ##. La pérdida no está en el render: está en la fuente.

Y hay un detalle que sí es un mecanismo, no un accidente: de los dos comentarios HTML del cuerpo publicado, el que

Kubernetes.title: Building a Kubernetes GitOps Lab with Argo CD: Installation, DNS Troubleshooting and Nginx Deployment
Kubernetes.summary:
Installing and Configuring Argo CD on Kubernetes | GitOps Lab

1. Overview

In this lab, I installed Argo CD on a two-node Kubernetes cluster using the official Argo CD installation manifest and configured it to deploy an Nginx application from a GitHub repository.

Argo CD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. It continuously monitors the desired application state stored in a Git repository and compares it with the actual state running inside the Kubernetes cluster.

When changes are committed to Git, Argo CD can automatically synchronize those changes with the Kubernetes cluster.

Lab environment

Component Configuration
Kubernetes cluster kubeadm
Control-plane node k8s
Control-plane IP 192.168.64.4
Worker node workernode2
Worker IP 192.168.64.5
Operating system Ubuntu 26.10 ARM64
Container runtime containerd
CNI Calico
Argo CD namespace argocd
Installation method Official stable manifest
Git repository GitHub
Application Nginx
Application namespace nginx-demo

2. Prerequisites

Before installing Argo CD, ensure:

  • Kubernetes cluster is initialized and operational.
  • kubectl is installed and configured.
  • All nodes are in Ready state.
  • CoreDNS is installed and running.
  • Cluster networking is functional.

Check the cluster:

kubectl get nodes -o wide

Check system pods:

kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide

3. Create the Argo CD namespace

We created a dedicated namespace to isolate Argo CD components from application workloads.

kubectl create namespace argocd

Verify:

kubectl get namespaces

Why a separate namespace?

  • Keeps Argo CD components logically isolated.
  • Makes resource management easier.
  • Allows namespace-level monitoring and troubleshooting.
  • Provides a dedicated location for Argo CD secrets and configuration.

4. Install Argo CD

We used the official Argo CD installation manifest from the stable release channel.

kubectl apply -n argocd \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

This manifest installs the Argo CD components and their required Kubernetes resources, including:

  • Deployments
  • Services
  • ConfigMaps
  • Secrets
  • ServiceAccounts
  • RBAC resources
  • Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)

The standard installation includes the components required for the Argo CD UI, API, repository access, and application reconciliation.

5. Verify the installation

Check all Argo CD pods:

kubectl get pods -n argocd -o wide

Check deployments:

kubectl get deployments -n argocd

Check services:

kubectl get services -n argocd

Check all resources:

kubectl get all -n argocd

In our lab, all seven Argo CD pods reached the Running state with containers Ready.

Important Argo CD components

Component Responsibility
argocd-server API server and web UI
argocd-repo-server Clones Git repositories and generates application manifests
argocd-application-controller Monitors applications and reconciles desired state
argocd-dex-server Identity integration
argocd-redis Caching
argocd-applicationset-controller Generates and manages applications from ApplicationSet resources
argocd-notifications-controller Application event notifications

6. Access the Argo CD web UI

By default, Argo CD's server is not exposed externally through a LoadBalancer or Ingress.

For our local Kubernetes lab, we used kubectl port-forward.

Run:

kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server \
  -n argocd 8080:443 \
  --address 0.0.0.0

Explanation:

  • svc/argocd-server: Targets the Argo CD server Service.
  • -n argocd: Selects the Argo CD namespace.
  • 8080:443: Maps port 8080 on the VM to HTTPS port 443 on the Service.
  • --address 0.0.0.0: Allows connections to the forwarded port through the VM's network interfaces.

Keep this terminal running while accessing the UI.

Open the following URL from the Mac:

https://192.168.64.4:8080

The default installation uses a self-signed TLS certificate, so the browser may display a certificate warning. This is expected for the initial lab setup.

Security note: Binding to 0.0.0.0 exposes the forwarded port on all VM interfaces. Use this only in a controlled lab network. For a more restricted setup, bind to 127.0.0.1 and access through an appropriate tunnel.

7. Retrieve the initial admin password

Argo CD generates an initial password for its admin account and stores it in a Kubernetes Secret.

Retrieve it using:

kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
  -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d; echo

Login credentials:

Username: admin
Password: Output of the previous command

Enter these credentials in the Argo CD web UI.

Security recommendation: Change the initial admin password after the first login. Once the password has been changed, delete the initial password Secret:

kubectl delete secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -n argocd

8. Connect Argo CD to a Git repository

After installation, the next step is to connect Argo CD to a Git repository containing Kubernetes manifests.

For our lab, we used:

GitHub repository:

https://github.com/mhasif0786/mhasifkamal-infra.git

The repository contains the desired Kubernetes configuration.

Example repository structure:

mhasifkamal-infra/
│
├── apps/
│   └── nginx-demo/
│       ├── deployment.yaml
│       └── service.yaml
│
└── README.md

The application directory contains the Kubernetes manifests that Argo CD monitors.

9. Create the Nginx Kubernetes manifests

9.1 Deployment manifest

File: apps/nginx-demo/deployment.yaml

9.2 Service manifest

File: apps/nginx-demo/service.yaml

The Deployment maintains two Nginx pod replicas.

The Service provides a stable internal endpoint to access the Nginx pods.

Commit and push the manifests to GitHub before configuring the Argo CD application.

10. Create an Argo CD Application

We created an application named nginx-demo.

The application configuration was:

Setting Value
Application name nginx-demo
Project default
Repository URL https://github.com/mhasif0786/mhasifkamal-infra.git
Target revision HEAD
Path apps/nginx-demo
Destination cluster https://kubernetes.default.svc
Destination namespace nginx-demo
Sync policy Automatic
Auto-create namespace Enabled

Understanding the configuration

Repository URL: The Git repository containing the desired Kubernetes state.

Target revision: HEAD tells Argo CD to track the repository's current HEAD revision.

Path: Identifies the directory containing Kubernetes manifests.

Destination cluster: https://kubernetes.default.svc refers to the Kubernetes cluster where Argo CD is running.

Destination namespace: The namespace where the application resources should be deployed.

Automatic synchronization: Argo CD can automatically reconcile changes in Git with the cluster.

Auto-create namespace: Allows Argo CD to create the destination namespace if it does not already exist.

We used the existing default AppProject.

11. Troubleshooting: Argo CD could not access GitHub

During application creation, we encountered:

InvalidSpecError: repository not accessible

unable to ls-remote HEAD

Get "https://github.com/.../info/refs?service=git-upload-pack":

dial tcp: lookup github.com on 10.96.0.10:53:
server misbehaving

This indicated a DNS resolution failure rather than a Git authentication problem.

11.1 Check CoreDNS pods 

kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide

Both CoreDNS pods were Running.

However, Running status alone does not guarantee successful DNS resolution.

11.2 Inspect the CoreDNS configuration 

kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml

We found:

forward . /etc/resolv.conf {
    max_concurrent 1000
}

This forwards external DNS queries to the upstream resolvers listed in /etc/resolv.conf.

11.3 Inspect the node DNS configuration 

resolvectl status

The node had these upstream DNS servers:

192.168.64.1
fe80::8047:15ff:feae:f164%2

CoreDNS logs showed timeouts when forwarding queries to the IPv4 resolver and an error when using the IPv6 link-local resolver.

11.4 Compare DNS resolution from the host and pod

From the Kubernetes node:

nslookup github.com 192.168.64.1

This succeeded.

We then created a temporary diagnostic pod:

kubectl run dns-test \
  --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --restart=Never \
  --rm -it \
  --command -- sh

Inside the pod, we checked:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

The pod used:

nameserver 10.96.0.10

Internal DNS resolution worked:

nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local

But the direct query to the gateway DNS server failed:

nslookup github.com 192.168.64.1

We tested alternative upstream resolvers:

nslookup github.com 1.1.1.1
nslookup github.com 8.8.8.8

Both succeeded from the pod.

Root cause

The upstream resolvers inherited by CoreDNS were not usable from the CoreDNS pod network for external DNS queries.

The host could resolve external domains, but the CoreDNS pods could not successfully use the same upstream resolvers.

11.5 Correct the CoreDNS forwarding configuration

We updated the CoreDNS ConfigMap.

Previous configuration:

forward . /etc/resolv.conf {
    max_concurrent 1000
}

Updated configuration:

forward . 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 {
    max_concurrent 1000
}

Why did we change it?

The original configuration dynamically reads upstream DNS servers from /etc/resolv.conf. However, the inherited resolver configuration was not working from the CoreDNS pod network.

We verified that 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 were reachable and returned valid DNS responses from a Kubernetes diagnostic pod.

We therefore configured CoreDNS to use these verified upstream resolvers directly.

11.6 Restart CoreDNS

After updating the ConfigMap, we restarted the CoreDNS deployment:

kubectl rollout restart deployment/coredns -n kube-system

Wait for the rollout:

kubectl rollout status deployment/coredns -n kube-system

Check the pods:

kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide

11.7 Validate DNS resolution

We used a fresh diagnostic pod to validate external and internal DNS resolution.

kubectl run dns-test \
  --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --restart=Never \
  --rm -it \
  --command -- sh

Inside the pod:

External DNS:

nslookup github.com

Internal Kubernetes DNS:

nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local

Both internal and external DNS resolution should work.

Resolution

The CoreDNS forwarding configuration was corrected to use reachable upstream DNS servers rather than the inherited resolver configuration.

The DNS configuration correction was applied, and CoreDNS was restarted.

Following this correction, Argo CD successfully accessed the GitHub repository and synchronized the application.

12. Verify Argo CD repository connectivity and application status

After correcting DNS, the nginx-demo application successfully synchronized.

We verified the application status in the Argo CD UI.

Argo CD dashboard result

Property Observed status
Application nginx-demo
Project default
Sync status Synced
Health status Healthy
Operation status Sync OK
Repository https://github.com/mhasif0786/mhasifkamal-infra.git
Target revision HEAD
Manifest path apps/nginx-demo
Destination in-cluster
Namespace nginx-demo

The dashboard showed:

  • Synced: 1
  • Healthy: 1
  • Sync OK: 1
  • OutOfSync: 0
  • Degraded: 0
  • Sync errors: 0

What this confirms

  • Argo CD successfully accessed the Git repository.
  • Repository manifest retrieval and application processing succeeded.
  • The application synchronization operation completed successfully.
  • Argo CD reports the application as Healthy and Synced.
  • The previous external DNS resolution issue no longer prevents this GitOps workflow.

Useful commands:

kubectl get applications -n argocd

kubectl describe application nginx-demo -n argocd

If repository connectivity problems occur again:

kubectl logs deployment/argocd-repo-server -n argocd

13. Verify the Nginx application in Kubernetes

After successful synchronization, we verified the actual Kubernetes resources from the control-plane node.

13.1 Check all application resources 

kubectl get all -n nginx-demo -o wide

Actual output:

NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP                NODE
pod/nginx-68d7965994-8xdrh   1/1     Running   0          19m   192.168.216.82   workernode2
pod/nginx-68d7965994-j5xf5   1/1     Running   0          19m   192.168.216.83   workernode2

NAME            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
service/nginx   ClusterIP   10.110.116.36           80/TCP

NAME                    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
deployment.apps/nginx   2/2     2            2           19m

NAME                               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
replicaset.apps/nginx-68d7965994   2         2         2

13.2 Deployment verification 

kubectl get deployment nginx -n nginx-demo

Observed state:

NAME    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
nginx   2/2     2            2

The Deployment successfully maintains two replicas.

  • Desired replicas: 2
  • Current replicas: 2
  • Ready replicas: 2
  • Available replicas: 2

13.3 Pod verification

Observed pods:

NAME                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP                NODE
nginx-68d7965994-8xdrh   1/1     Running   0          19m   192.168.216.82   workernode2
nginx-68d7965994-j5xf5   1/1     Running   0          19m   192.168.216.83   workernode2

Both Nginx pods are:

  • Running and Ready (1/1).
  • Running without container restarts.
  • Assigned unique Pod IP addresses.
  • Scheduled on the workernode2 worker node.

13.4 Service verification

Observed Service:

NAME    TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
nginx   ClusterIP   10.110.116.36           80/TCP

Service configuration:

  • Service name: nginx
  • Type: ClusterIP
  • Cluster IP: 10.110.116.36
  • Service port: 80
  • Selector: app=nginx

The Service provides a stable internal endpoint for accessing the Nginx pods.

13.5 ReplicaSet verification

Observed ReplicaSet:

NAME                     DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
nginx-68d7965994          2         2         2

The ReplicaSet is responsible for maintaining the desired number of Nginx pod replicas.

13.6 Understanding the request flow 

                 Client / Application
                         |
                         |
                         v
                Nginx ClusterIP Service
                  10.110.116.36:80
                         |
                 Service Selector
                    app=nginx
                         |
                 +-------+-------+
                 |               |
                 v               v
           Nginx Pod 1      Nginx Pod 2
           192.168.216.82   192.168.216.83
                 |               |
                 +-------+-------+
                         |
                     workernode2

The Kubernetes Service selects pods using the label app=nginx and makes them available through a stable ClusterIP endpoint.

14. Additional Kubernetes verification commands

Check the Deployment:

kubectl get deployment nginx -n nginx-demo

Check pods and their node placement:

kubectl get pods -n nginx-demo -o wide

Check the Service:

kubectl get svc nginx -n nginx-demo

Check Service endpoints:

kubectl get endpoints nginx -n nginx-demo

Check EndpointSlices:

kubectl get endpointslices -n nginx-demo

Check rollout status:

kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx -n nginx-demo

15. Understanding the GitOps workflow

The complete workflow in this lab:

Developer
    |
    | Changes Kubernetes YAML
    v
GitHub Repository
    |
    | New commit
    v
Argo CD Repo Server
    |
    | Fetches Git repository
    | Reads Kubernetes manifests
    v
Argo CD Application Controller
    |
    | Compares desired state with actual state
    | Detects differences
    v
Kubernetes API Server
    |
    | Applies desired resources
    v
nginx-demo Namespace
    |
    +---- Nginx Deployment
    |
    +---- Nginx ReplicaSet
    |
    +---- Nginx Pods (2 replicas)
    |
    +---- Nginx ClusterIP Service

Desired state vs actual state

Desired state: The configuration stored in Git.

Actual state: The resources currently running in Kubernetes.

Argo CD continuously compares these two states and reports whether the application is Synced or OutOfSync.

When automated synchronization is configured, Argo CD can apply changes from Git to bring the cluster back toward the desired state.

16. Current Lab Status

Component Status
Kubernetes cluster Operational
Argo CD installation Successful
Argo CD UI Accessible
GitHub repository connection Successful
CoreDNS external forwarding correction Applied
Argo CD application sync Synced
Application health Healthy
Nginx Deployment 2/2 Available
Nginx pods 2/2 Running
Nginx Service ClusterIP created
Nginx ReplicaSet 2/2 Ready

Result: Successfully deployed a two-replica Nginx application using Argo CD and a GitHub-hosted Kubernetes manifest repository. Verified the Deployment, ReplicaSet, pods, and Service directly through Kubernetes.

17. Next Steps and Experiments

The next experiments will focus on understanding GitOps reconciliation and Kubernetes production behavior.

17.1 Git-driven scaling

Change the replica count in Git from two to three:

spec:
  replicas: 3

Commit and push:

git add .
git commit -m "Increase nginx replicas to 3"
git push origin main

Observe Argo CD detecting the Git change and synchronizing the updated desired state.

Verify:

kubectl get deployment nginx -n nginx-demo

kubectl get pods -n nginx-demo

Expected deployment state:

nginx   3/3

17.2 Drift detection

Manually change the live Kubernetes state:

kubectl scale deployment nginx \
  --replicas=2 \
  -n nginx-demo

If Git still declares three replicas, observe how Argo CD detects the difference.

This experiment helps distinguish desired state from actual state.

17.3 Self-healing

Enable and test automated self-healing through Argo CD.

Observe whether manual changes to the live cluster are automatically reverted to match the Git repository.

17.4 Service connectivity

Test Nginx through its ClusterIP from a temporary test pod.

kubectl run curl-test \
  --image=curlimages/curl \
  --restart=Never \
  --rm -it \
  --command -- sh

Inside the pod:

curl http://nginx.nginx-demo.svc.cluster.local

Expected result: Nginx welcome page HTML.

17.5 Rolling updates

Change the Nginx image version in Git and observe the Deployment rollout.

kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx -n nginx-demo

Inspect rollout history:

kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx -n nginx-demo

Kubernetes.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Weights Drop Nov 4: Licence, Size, How to Run
Kubernetes.summary:
On November 4, 2026, Moonshot AI is scheduled to do something no lab has done before: hand the public the complete weights of a 2.8-trillion-parameter AI model that independent testing currently ranks as the strongest open model in the world. Kimi K3.1 Pro has been live through Moonshot's apps and API since October 23, but the downloadable release — the one that lets anyone outside Moonshot run, inspect, fine-tune and redistribute the model — is still a promise with a date on it. We checked Moonshot's Hugging Face organisation while writing this article: there is no K3.1 Pro repository yet. The newest thing there is still the older Kimi K3. So this is the guide to read before the drop: what exactly is landing, the licence question that will decide what "open" really means here, the terabyte-scale hardware reality, the two controversies hanging over the release, and a checklist for the day itself. For the launch story — benchmarks, pricing and how the model performs — start with our Kimi K3.1 Pro launch guide; this article is about the weights.

What exactly is dropping on November 4

Kimi K3.1 Pro is not a new architecture. It is a heavily post-trained version of Kimi K3, the model Moonshot released in the summer: a mixture-of-experts system with 2.8 trillion total parameters, of which about 104 billion are active on any given token. It uses Moonshot's Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals design, reads text, images and video in a single model, and works across a context window of one million tokens. What the extra post-training bought is measurable: on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, K3 scored 44; K3.1 Pro scores 55, fourth of every model the evaluator tracks and only three points behind the best closed model, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5.

"Full model weights" is the phrase that matters. A weight file is the trained model itself — the numbers that encode everything it learned. With the weights, the model stops being a service you rent from Moonshot and becomes a file you possess: you can run it on hardware you control, fine-tune it on your own data, inspect its behaviour without an API in between, and keep it forever even if Moonshot changes its prices, its terms, or its mind. That is why a weights release is a different event from an API launch, and why the October 23 launch, impressive as it was, is only half the story.

Two things about the drop are still unknown, and both matter. First, Moonshot has not said whether the faster K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant is part of the weights release or stays a hosted-only product. Second — and this is the big one — Moonshot has not named the licence. More on that below, because there is a very good precedent to read in the meantime.

Here is what the family looks like side by side. The K3 column is verified from the actual Hugging Face repository; the K3.1 Pro column is what is known or reasonably expected before November 4, and every expectation is labelled as one.

Kimi K3 (already out) Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights due Nov 4)
Total / active parameters 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion (same base)
Context window 1 million tokens 1 million tokens
Input Text, images, video Text, images, video
Weight format MXFP4 weights, MXFP8 activations Not yet published; MXFP4 expected
Download size on Hugging Face 1.56 TB across 96 files Not yet published; similar scale expected
Licence Kimi K3 License (custom) Not yet announced
Serving vLLM and SGLang, official recipes Not yet published; same stacks expected
API price $3 / $15 per million tokens $2 / $10 per million tokens

The licence question — and what K3's licence actually says

Everything about this release hinges on a document that does not exist yet. "Open weights" tells you the file is downloadable; it says nothing about what you are allowed to do with it. That is the licence's job, and Moonshot's announcement named none. The honest position today is: unknown, decided on November 4.

But we are not guessing in the dark, because Kimi K3 shipped under a licence Moonshot wrote for exactly this model family, and you can read it in full in the Kimi K3 repository on Hugging Face. It is a short, unusually readable document, and if K3.1 Pro follows the same pattern — which is an expectation, not a fact — this is what "open" will mean in practice.

The Kimi K3 License starts like the famous MIT licence: permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software — explicitly including the weights, the code and the right to fine-tune and build derivative works — free of charge. For researchers, hobbyists, and the overwhelming majority of companies, that is the whole story: download it and build.

Then come two conditions aimed at the very top of the market. The first is the "Model as a Service" clause. If you or your affiliates run a business that gives third parties API-style access to model inference or fine-tuning — where those third parties meaningfully control inputs, parameters or training data — and that business's aggregate revenue exceeds 20 million US dollars over any consecutive twelve months, you must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before using the model commercially. Note what the clause deliberately does not cover: products that merely embed the model inside specific features, and simple relays of requests to models hosted by others. The second condition is a branding rule: if the model powers a commercial product with more than 100 million monthly active users, or more than 20 million dollars in monthly revenue, the name "Kimi K3" must be prominently displayed in that product's interface.

A final carve-out softens both conditions: they do not apply to purely internal use — anything that never exposes the model, its outputs or its capabilities to third parties — nor to use through Moonshot's own products and certified inference partners. And the licence closes with the standard "as is" disclaimer and a contact address for licensing questions.

So when the K3.1 Pro licence appears, the checklist is short and specific. Is it the same Kimi K3 License with the name swapped, or a new document? Is the Model-as-a-Service revenue threshold still 20 million dollars? Does the branding rule survive? Has anything been added — an acceptable-use list, a geographic restriction, a research-only tier? Five minutes of reading on November 4 will answer all of it, and until those five minutes happen, any article that tells you what you may do with these weights — including confident claims that they are "fully open" or "not really open" — is getting ahead of the document.

One and a half terabytes: the hardware reality

The second reality check is physical. The Kimi K3 weights on Hugging Face occupy 1.56 terabytes, spread across 96 files, in MXFP4 format — a compact 4-bit representation that Moonshot bakes in during training rather than squeezing down afterwards. K3.1 Pro is the same architecture at the same parameter count, so a similar footprint is the reasonable expectation. To put 1.56 terabytes in perspective: it is roughly twenty-five times the size of a typical 70-billion-parameter model download, and it will not fit on the drive of most workstations, let alone in the memory of a gaming GPU.

Running it is a data-centre conversation, and the arithmetic is not complicated. The weights alone need about 1.6 terabytes of fast memory before you have processed a single token; on top of that sits the key-value cache for that million-token context, which grows with every conversation you serve. A top-end data-centre GPU carries around 141 to 192 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory. Divide the weights by that and you land in the region of ten to twelve flagship GPUs just to hold the model — one full high-end server node, or a couple of smaller ones linked together — with more headroom needed for comfortable serving. This is not a criticism; it is the honest category of the thing. K3.1 Pro is open in the sense that a power station's blueprints are open: nothing stops you, provided you have a power station.

Three practical consequences follow. First, the first wave of real usage will come from inference providers and well-equipped labs, not individuals — watch for hosted endpoints appearing within days of the drop, the same pattern that followed the Mistral Large 4 open-weights release in late October. Second, community quantisation projects will immediately try to squeeze the model smaller; how much intelligence survives aggressive shrinking of a model that is already 4-bit native is a genuine open question, and early claims should be treated as claims. Third, for almost everyone reading this, the API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens will remain the rational way to use K3.1 Pro for the foreseeable future — the weights matter to you because they cap Moonshot's pricing power and guarantee the model's survival, not because you will host it yourself.

How you will actually run it

If you do have the hardware, the path is already paved, because K3 set it up. Moonshot's K3 release shipped with official support in the two serving stacks that dominate open-model deployment: vLLM, which carries a Moonshot-maintained recipe for the model, and SGLang, which documents it in its cookbook. Day-one support for K3.1 Pro in the same stacks is the reasonable expectation — the architecture is unchanged — but "reasonable expectation" is doing real work in that sentence, and the model card on November 4 is the document that will confirm versions, flags and known issues.

Preparation, if you intend to be ready on the day, is mostly logistics. You need roughly 1.6 terabytes of fast local storage free, a Hugging Face account that has accepted any licence gate the repository carries, and your serving stack installed and tested in advance — K3 itself is the perfect rehearsal download if bandwidth is cheap for you, since its tooling, file layout and deployment guides mirror what is coming. One warning from experience with every major drop: the first hours bring download congestion and a flood of re-uploads, mirrors and repackaged versions from unknown accounts. Download from the official moonshotai organisation only, and let other people be the first to discover which community conversion is broken.

The scoreboard moved: Index v5 and the speed problem

Anyone preparing to evaluate the drop should know that the measuring stick changed last week. On October 27, Artificial Analysis replaced its Intelligence Index with version 5, built mostly on private tests. Under the new index, K3.1 Pro scores 46 — ninth overall, and the highest score of any open-weights model, three points behind the best closed systems on that chart. Some of Artificial Analysis's own task-level measurements are striking: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, the tough terminal-based coding-agent test, they measured K3.1 Pro at 67 percent — the highest they had recorded — and on their GDPval-AA measure of economically valuable knowledge work it ranks third. Moonshot's own reported Terminal-Bench figure, 65.7 percent against Claude Opus 5.5's 66.4, is close behind.

The same independent testing exposes the model's real weakness, and it is not intelligence. It is speed. Artificial Analysis measured K3.1 Pro's output at about 41 tokens per second, ranking 188th of 192 models for output speed. For batch work and offline analysis that hardly matters. For interactive products — a coding assistant answering in real time, an agent loop making hundreds of calls — it matters a great deal, and it is part of why OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra, launched October 26 at half the per-token price of the model it replaces and scoring 48 on the new index, is a serious rival for the same workloads. The Highspeed variant exists precisely because Moonshot knows this; whether self-hosting the weights improves or worsens the speed picture will be one of the first things the community benchmarks after November 4. Our comparison of the best AI coding assistants is a useful map of the field this model is entering.

Two controversies hanging over the drop

An honest preview has to include the two stories that broke around this model in the last week, labelled for exactly what they are.

The first is a report, not a finding. On October 28, The Information reported — and Reuters followed on October 29 — that according to people with direct knowledge, Moonshot relied heavily on outputs from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to train K3.1 Pro, with a similar claim made about DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash. Training one model on another's outputs, called distillation, sits in contested legal and ethical territory and is restricted by most providers' terms. What is established: the report exists, it is attributed to unnamed sources, and as of October 29 neither Moonshot, OpenAI nor DeepSeek had publicly commented on it. What is not established: whether it is true, and if so, to what degree. It changes nothing about the file that lands on November 4, but it may shape how enterprises' lawyers read the licence — one more reason that document matters.

The second story is Moonshot's own disclosure, and it is stranger: for the open-weight release, the company deliberately made its model worse at hacking. Moonshot says it identified and removed cyberattack-related material from both the mid-training data and the reinforcement-learning tasks, because capability at finding and exploiting software flaws was rising with scale and weights, once published, cannot be recalled. On its internal exploit benchmark, the filtered model scores 81.0 percent; an identical pipeline without the filtering scores 90.5 percent. Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin publicly defended the approach, arguing that restraint now beats the identity-check regimes that a wave of AI-powered attacks could trigger. The open question — and it can only be answered after November 4 — is whether the reduction survives contact with the research community: outside teams will test whether fine-tuning restores the removed capability, and at least one company has already publicly announced plans to try stripping the safeguards. Moonshot's published before-and-after numbers make this the first open release in history whose safety claim arrives with its own test attached.

A third, smaller allegation deserves a sentence for completeness: VentureBeat reported screenshots, which it could not authenticate, purporting to show a paid-promotion brief for Kimi creators that included an instruction not to label posts as paid partnerships. Moonshot had not responded in the reporting. Unverified documents are not evidence — but if you see suspiciously synchronised praise on drop day, you will know the context in which to read it.

Meanwhile, K2 closes its doors today

One dated detail is easy to miss in the drop coverage: the previous generation is being retired on a schedule that starts now. Moonshot's pricing pages indicate the K2 series closes to new users from October 31 — today — and is due to be fully retired by the end of December. If your product still routes traffic to a K2 model, the weights drop is not your only November deadline; migration to K3 or K3.1 Pro belongs on the same calendar page. Moonshot also had a smaller operational stumble this week, apologising for rate limits on K3.1 Pro and resetting a portion of user quotas — a useful reminder that demand for this model, even hosted, is currently outrunning the supply pointed at it.

Your November 4 checklist

When the repository appears, these are the checks that separate knowing from repeating — the same checks we will run before updating this article:

  1. The licence file. Name, Model-as-a-Service threshold, branding rule, anything new. Read the document, not the summaries.
  2. The repository itself. Official moonshotai organisation, exact repo names — and whether Highspeed is included or hosted-only.
  3. Formats and size. MXFP4 as expected? Total terabytes? Any official smaller variants?
  4. The model card. Shipped context length, serving-stack versions, known limitations, and any stated difference between the API model and the released weights.
  5. Independent numbers. Artificial Analysis and community evaluations run on the released weights — not the API — including whether the cyber-capability reduction is measurable.
  6. First endpoints. Which inference providers list it, at what price per token, within the first week.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are the Kimi K3.1 Pro weights out now?

No. As of October 31, 2026, Moonshot's Hugging Face organisation has no K3.1 Pro repository — the newest release there is still Kimi K3. Moonshot's announcement promises the full weights "will be released by Nov 4, 2026", and until the repository appears, the model is available only through Kimi's apps and Moonshot's API.

What licence will the K3.1 Pro weights use?

Moonshot has not announced one. The best guide is the precedent: Kimi K3 shipped under the custom Kimi K3 License — broadly MIT-style freedom to use, modify and sell, with a separate-agreement requirement for Model-as-a-Service businesses earning over $20 million a year, and a branding rule for products above 100 million monthly users or $20 million in monthly revenue. Whether K3.1 Pro uses the same licence can only be confirmed from the licence file in its repository on November 4.

How big will the download be?

Kimi K3's weights occupy 1.56 terabytes on Hugging Face in MXFP4 format across 96 files. K3.1 Pro shares the same 2.8-trillion-parameter architecture, so a similar size is expected — but the exact figure is only known when the repository is published. Plan for roughly 1.6 terabytes of free, fast storage.

Can I run Kimi K3.1 Pro on my own computer?

Realistically, no — and that is about physics, not permission. The weights alone need around 1.6 terabytes of memory to load, which means roughly ten to twelve flagship data-centre GPUs before serving a single request. Community quantisation projects will try to shrink it after release, but a model that is already natively 4-bit has limited room to shrink. For individuals and most teams, the API at $2/$10 per million tokens is the practical route.

Is it true K3.1 Pro was trained on GPT-6 outputs?

It has been reported, not proven. The Information reported on October 28, 2026, citing people with direct knowledge, that Moonshot relied heavily on GPT-6 Astra outputs to train K3.1 Pro; Reuters carried the report on October 29. Moonshot, OpenAI and DeepSeek had issued no public comment as of October 29. Treat the claim as an unconfirmed allegation until a company statement or stronger evidence appears.

Conclusion

Strip away the hype and November 4 is a document release as much as a model release. The model itself is already proven in public: fourth on the old independent index, top of the open field on the new one, priced a third below its predecessor, and slow enough that speed — not smarts — is its honest weakness. What nobody outside Moonshot has seen is the paperwork and the files: the licence that decides whether "open" means MIT-free or free-with-conditions, the repository that decides whether Highspeed is included, and the released weights that decide whether the much-discussed cyber-capability reduction is real. Our launch guide covers what K3.1 Pro is; this article will be updated with what the drop actually contained — licence first — as soon as the repository is live and verified. If Moonshot keeps its date, that update lands on November 4.

Rust.title: Hybrid search in Python: BM25 + vectors with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, alpha swept 0 to 1
Rust.summary:
Should you fuse BM25 with vector search, and what weight should each side get? I ran both retrievers separately and fused them with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) across three different query styles, sweeping the fusion weight from pure vector to pure BM25.

Result: no single retriever wins everywhere. Pure BM25 beat pure vectors by 49 points of MRR on exact code identifiers (0.772 vs 0.279). Pure vectors beat pure BM25 by 24 points on hand-written paraphrase questions (0.768 vs 0.566). An RRF blend with 80% weight on BM25 rank was the only setting that stayed within 9 points of the best score on every query type.

The setup

  • Corpus: the English FastAPI docs, 151 Markdown files, chunked with the heading-aware-plus-heading-path chunker from my chunking benchmark, the strategy that scored best there. 2,713 chunks.
  • BM25: the same from-scratch implementation as the chunking post (k1=1.5, b=0.75), reused unchanged.
  • Vectors: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 384 dimensions, cosine similarity via normalized dot product. A small, CPU-friendly model (model card).
  • Fusion: score(d) = alpha / (60 + rank_bm25(d)) + (1 - alpha) / (60 + rank_vec(d)). Standard RRF with k=60, the constant from the original Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher paper, with a weight alpha instead of a flat 50/50 sum. alpha=1.0 is pure BM25, alpha=0.0 is pure vector search. Each retriever contributes its own top 50 candidates; a document missing from one side gets rank 200 for that side's term.
  • Three query sets, on purpose:
    1. Heading queries (773): section headings used verbatim. They overlap with the indexed heading-path prefix by construction, so this is an easy benchmark, kept for continuity, not as the main result.
    2. Identifier queries (305): inline-code spans like response_model or BackgroundTasks that appear in exactly one chunk. This tests exact-token recall, the case hybrid search is usually sold on.
    3. Paraphrase queries (30): questions I wrote by hand, like "How do I run code after sending the response to the client?" for the background-tasks page, avoiding the target page's own vocabulary. A hit counts any chunk from the target file. Small sample, so treat the percentages as approximate.

Results

MRR by alpha (0.0 = pure vector, 1.0 = pure BM25):

alpha heading MRR identifier MRR paraphrase MRR
0.0 0.491 0.279 0.768
0.2 0.581 0.471 0.794
0.4 0.642 0.569 0.806
0.5 0.679 0.696 0.751
0.6 0.710 0.735 0.731
0.8 0.782 0.753 0.722
0.9 0.813 0.768 0.678
1.0 0.859 0.772 0.566

hit@1 / hit@5 for the identifier and paraphrase sets:

alpha identifier hit@1 identifier hit@5 paraphrase hit@1 paraphrase hit@5
0.0 0.207 0.397 0.667 0.933
0.4 0.515 0.656 0.667 0.967
0.8 0.662 0.889 0.533 0.933
1.0 0.692 0.889 0.367 0.867

What the numbers mean

BM25 wins big on identifiers, vectors win big on paraphrases, by more than I guessed. MiniLM's hit@1 on identifier queries was 0.207. A 384-dim sentence model wasn't trained to preserve rare exact tokens like BackgroundTasks; it embeds the gist of the sentence around it, and one API reference page looks a lot like another. BM25's IDF weighting does the opposite: a rare token dominates the score.

Pure BM25 also won the heading benchmark, and that number is misleading. The chunker prepends each chunk's heading path to the indexed text, so querying with the heading is close to a substring search, BM25's best case. Real users don't type section titles. The 30 paraphrase questions are the fairer read on "does semantic search help", and there pure vectors beat pure BM25 by 24 MRR points.

No fixed alpha is best for all three. alpha=0.4 is best for paraphrases, alpha=1.0 for identifiers and headings. Taking the worst-case regret across the three query types, the minimum is at alpha=0.8: 1.9 points below the best identifier score, 8.4 below the best paraphrase score, 7.7 below the best heading score. alpha=0.5, the "obvious" 50/50 choice, loses 18 points on headings.

Honest caveats

  • The paraphrase set is small and I wrote it. 30 questions is enough to see a 24-point gap, not enough to trust the third decimal place.
  • The heading benchmark favors whatever puts the query text into the index, BM25's easiest case.
  • One small local embedding model. Larger or API-hosted embedding models could close some of the identifier gap. I didn't test that.
  • RRF's k=60 wasn't swept here. Only alpha was. (I did sweep k in a follow-up.)
  • Single corpus. FastAPI's docs are unusually well structured. A messier corpus would likely show a smaller BM25 edge on identifiers.

The fusion code 

K_RRF = 60

def rrf_fuse(bm25_ranked_ids, vec_ranked_ids, alpha, top_k=5):
    """bm25_ranked_ids, vec_ranked_ids: lists of doc ids, best first.
    alpha=1.0 is pure BM25, alpha=0.0 is pure vector."""
    rank_bm = {doc_id: r for r, doc_id in enumerate(bm25_ranked_ids)}
    rank_vec = {doc_id: r for r, doc_id in enumerate(vec_ranked_ids)}
    fallback = max(len(bm25_ranked_ids), len(vec_ranked_ids)) * 4
    candidates = set(rank_bm) | set(rank_vec)
    scored = [
        (
            alpha / (K_RRF + rank_bm.get(d, fallback) + 1)
            + (1 - alpha) / (K_RRF + rank_vec.get(d, fallback) + 1),
            d,
        )
        for d in candidates
    ]
    scored.sort(reverse=True)
    return [d for _, d in scored[:top_k]]

Run BM25 and your vector index independently, each returning its own top-N (50 was enough here), then fuse. No score normalization needed: that's the point of using ranks instead of raw scores, which differ in scale between BM25 and cosine similarity.

Latency on 2 vCPUs over 2,713 chunks: BM25 1.82 ms median, vector encode+search 23.99 ms. A hybrid query costs roughly what the vector half costs.

What I'd do in your pipeline

  1. Don't default to alpha=0.5. On this corpus it lost more than any other tested value on at least one query type. Start from 0.7-0.8 (BM25-leaning) and tune on a real query log.
  2. If your users type API names, error codes or config keys, weight BM25 heavily. Small embedding models are bad at exact tokens; that's structural, not a tuning problem.
  3. If your users type full questions, don't skip vectors. BM25 alone lost 24 MRR points on plain paraphrases.
  4. Measure your own alpha with a golden-set eval in CI built from real traffic instead of a guess.

The full script (bench_hybrid.py), raw results and corpus fetch script are on the original post.
